items.quote: those who study Physick, who are the Priests and Ministers of the Muses, and are marryed to their study in a godly wedlock
items.note: Croll addresses students of Physick and names them Priests and Ministers of the Muses, wedded to their study.

items.quote: the Paracelsian Theory of Chymicall Physick as yet is wrapt up in perplexities and some obscurities which are not easie to all
items.note: The text says the Paracelsian theory is as yet wrapped in perplexities and obscurities not easy to all.

items.quote: they would not be so shy to black their hands, but learn of Paracelsus and other Chymists to prepare and make up their Medicines, but to observe the method of Hippocrates in curing diseases
items.note: Croll's advice: learn the preparing of medicines from Paracelsus and the Chymists, keep the method of Hippocrates in curing.

items.quote: these two Schools of Old and New Physick may be reconcil'd without contradiction, and consist very well in a Physitian
items.note: Croll holds that the old and the new Physick can be reconciled in one physician.

items.quote: that over-grown damnable Custome of our time is worn out, according to which men use indifferently to dislike and reject the good with the bad
items.note: Croll condemns the custom of his time of rejecting the good together with the bad.

items.quote: as yet is wrapt up in perplexities and some obscurities which are not easie to all
items.note: The paragraph calls the Paracelsian theory wrapped in obscurities; the margin note to CH5.62 says 'Paracelsus would not have Physick be concealed'. The lines given do not settle how the two stand together.

items.quote: avoyd idlenes because it is the Devils cushon, the mother of vice & the step-mother of virtue
items.note: Margin note: idleness is to be avoided; work for the neighbour's good.

items.quote: Beginning with small things we should by little and little go on to greater things.
items.note: Margin note: one goes from small things step by step to greater.

items.quote: By the contempt of sciences we lose the good and get the evill.
items.note: Margin note: contempt of sciences loses the good and gains the evil.

items.quote: if he administer any thing it is to be accounted of as the hand of God
items.note: What an honest and able physician gives is to be counted the hand of God.

items.quote: in whom besides a fidutiall feare of God and Love to his sick neighbour, a singular Conscience and Experience is also requisite
items.note: What Croll requires in an honest and able physician: fear of God, love of the sick neighbour, conscience, experience.

items.quote: if he be a wretched Miscreant, and an Ignoramus, what he giveth is to be lookt upon as poyson
items.note: What a wicked and ignorant physician gives is to be looked on as poison.

items.quote: cannot indure that Physick with its preparations should premiscuously be imparted to all sorts of men, for fear if it should be made common, or as they say Prophaned, they should lose their gaines
items.note: Croll reports that a great part of physicians want Physick and its preparations withheld from the many, for fear of losing gain.

items.quote: or as they say Prophaned
items.name: great part of Physitians
items.note: The word 'Prophaned' for making Physick common is given to those physicians, not to Croll.

items.quote: tis a foolish conceit of the frantick vulgar sort, who think that a Secret looseth its vertue when tis made known
items.note: Croll rejects, as a conceit of the vulgar, the view that a secret loses its virtue when made known.

items.quote: those greedy covetous gaine-getters will cease their murmuring and forbear to curse and wish my eyes out for my good will
items.note: Croll speaks of his own good will in imparting Physick and of those who curse him for it.

items.quote: neither God nor Nature hath made every man a Physitian,
items.note: Croll's ground why making Physick known does no harm to physicians: not every man is made a physician.

items.quote: as one saddle will not fit every horse, nor can a child handle his weapon like a fencer
items.note: Two likenesses for the same point: a known medicine rightly given does not make the giver a physician.

items.quote: imitate that most commendable and religious custome of the Hermetick Physitians, who always use to pray for a blessing upon their endeavours
items.note: Croll commends the custom of the Hermetick Physitians of praying for a blessing on their work.

items.quote: Whosoever useth any Creature without craving a blissing, God imputeth it to him for no other than theft and rapine.
items.note: Using any creature without asking a blessing is counted by God as theft.

items.quote: Wee who professe CHRIST ought to administer in that Wonderfull Name of JESU
items.note: Croll: Christians ought to administer medicine in the name of Jesus.

items.quote: for so the Doctor of the Gentiles commandeth the Colossians, saying; Whatsoever yee do in word or deed,
items.name: the Doctor of the Gentiles
items.note: Words given to 'the Doctor of the Gentiles' writing to the Colossians, brought in support.

items.quote: Call upon me in the day of thy trouble, I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorifie me, saith our Creator
items.name: our Creator
items.note: Words given to 'our Creator', for the point that God's blessing is obtained by prayer.

items.quote: The best and chiefest Foundation of Physick is faith in God, and love to our neighbour, if this be wanting all Art is nothing worth.
items.note: Margin note names faith in God and love to the neighbour the foundation of Physick.

items.quote: Paracelsus would not have Physick be concealed.
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Margin note gives Paracelsus the view that Physick should not be concealed.

items.quote: though all experiences are secrets, yet Novices know not the Dose and true quantity in which the vertue of Physick consisteth
items.note: Margin note: all experiences are secrets, yet the virtue of Physick lies in the dose, which novices do not know.

items.quote: if we take too much Saffron or Treacle it is poyson, if too little it will doe no good
items.note: Margin note's example of the dose: too much is poison, too little does nothing.

items.name: Col.; 1 Cor.
items.note: Margin note names the writings beside the words 'do all in the NAME of the LORD'.

items.quote: First, then before we give or take any Physick we are to pray to the good and great God
items.note: The first of two numbered points: prayer before giving or taking Physick.

items.quote: pray to the good and great God that the Physick which he hath ordained as the meanes, may work Divine and healthfull effects
items.note: The step described: before a medicine is given or taken, a prayer that it may work; the Physick is called the means God ordained.

items.quote: Secondly, after we have recovered and made them well, let us never cease to give him hearty thanks
items.note: The second numbered point: thanks to God after recovery.

items.quote: These two poynts are scarce thought of by most Physitians, which is the chief cause of thier ill successe
items.note: Croll gives the neglect of prayer and thanks as the chief cause of physicians' ill success, for which the Art is then blamed.

items.quote: though a Cathartick medicine doth work equally effectually in a knave as it doth in an honest man
items.note: A medicine works alike in a knave and an honest man; the text says God permits this.

items.quote: yet the end in both may be far different and unlike, for it may be healthfull to the one, and hurtfull to the other
items.note: The end of the same medicine may differ: healthful to one, hurtful to the other.

items.quote: For what medicine soever it be that is administred and taken without imploring the Divine Grace,
items.note: Any medicine taken without asking divine grace is said to turn to a worse harm for the impenitent unbeliever.

items.name: Ecel.
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside the statement on medicine taken without imploring grace.

items.quote: sometimes the sick person is not recovered by the best and fittest medicines that can be applyed, and that for these eight causes
items.note: The text announces eight causes why the best medicines sometimes do not recover the sick; they follow numbered.

items.quote: First, Because the Terme of Life approacheth, which cannot be prolong'd by any art or help of Man
items.note: First cause: the term of life is near.

items.quote: No Medicine can preserve the corruptible body from death, the wages and punishment of sin
items.note: No medicine keeps the body from death, which is called the punishment of sin.

items.quote: there is one thing that hindereth corruption, reneweth youth, and prolongeth the short life, as in the Patriarchs
items.what: one thing that hindereth corruption, reneweth youth, and prolongeth the short life
items.note: The text sets apart 'one thing' with three effects and the Patriarchs as example; the lines given do not name it.

items.quote: as we shall shew anon, the life may be shortned or lengthned
items.note: Points forward to a later place in this writing on shortening and lengthening life.

items.quote: which cannot be prolong'd by any art or help of Man
items.note: The same paragraph says the term of life cannot be prolonged by art and that 'the life may be shortned or lengthned'; the text joins them with 'But although ... yet' (death at last is necessary).

items.quote: least with Plato we conclude a recesse after such a time
items.name: Plato
items.note: A view of a 'recesse after such a time' is given to Plato and set aside by Croll.

items.quote: for the conjunction of divers things necessarily implies a dissolution;
items.note: Croll's reason why death is necessary: what is joined of several things must be dissolved.

items.quote: And in this case the universall and chiefest medicine is of no effect, because no industry or skill of Artist or Nature can perpetuate the wedlock of life and death
items.note: Even 'the universall and chiefest medicine' is said to be of no effect against the appointed end.

items.quote: we are not therefore to desire, much lesse may we think to find any help beyond that utmost bound which God hath set us
items.note: No help is to be sought beyond the bound God has set.

items.quote: Paracels. lib. de resuscitatione naturalium, sol. 295.
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: Margin note names a writing of Paracelsus at the head of the first cause.

items.quote: The Curse in the Creature is removed by death.
items.note: Margin note: death removes the curse in the creature; it also speaks of a 'domestick enemy' as the cause of our death.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside the passage on the necessity of death.

items.quote: Secondly, Because through the ignorance of unskilfull Physitians, and their naughty medicines, the sick is brought to that passe, that the disease is corrupt, pernicious, and incurable
items.note: Second cause: unskilful physicians and bad medicines have made the disease incurable.

items.quote: And to such commonly the Chymists are sent for,
items.note: Croll says the Chymists are commonly called to cases already spoiled by others.

items.quote: whom Plutarch calls Physitians of Trophilus, who said that he was a compleat Physitian who could judg what might be done, and what not
items.name: Plutarch
items.note: A name for such physicians is given to Plutarch, and to Trophilus the saying on the complete physician.

items.quote: such never make use of their noble and undeserved Remedies, with a vaunting ostentation to their disgrace, when the sick is past all hope of mans help
items.note: Such physicians do not spend their remedies on a case past help.

items.quote: Let them take heed also they mix not their own medicines with others poyson, least the miscarriage be ascribed to the good and the recovery to the bad
items.note: Croll's warning: do not mix one's own medicines with those of others, lest blame and credit be misplaced.

items.quote: such as these men commonly (and justly) call Honest Hangmen
items.name: men
items.note: The name 'Honest Hangmen' for physicians who let a patient perish out of envy is given to common speech; Croll adds 'justly'.

items.quote: Thirdly, Because the Physitian is sent for too late, when Nature is overcome and the disease hath got the mastery
items.note: Third cause: the physician is called too late.

items.quote: resisting the disease at first, no doubt but by Gods blessing the expected fruit of health would have sprung up
items.note: Physick given in season, at the start of the disease, would have brought health; said in the figure of sowing and fruit.

items.quote: Fourthly, Because the sick doth not follow directions
items.note: Fourth cause: the sick does not follow directions.

items.quote: contrary to the Golden law of the Locrians recorded by Aelianus
items.name: Aelianus
items.note: A 'Golden law of the Locrians' is cited as recorded by Aelianus; the lines given do not state the law.

items.quote: Fifthly, Because some mens Natures or peculiar qualityes are not so easy to be cured
items.note: Fifth cause: some natures are hard to cure; likened to hard knotty wood.

items.quote: very often the Time or Season, together with the bad inclination of the Astra's is very crosse and contrary to the health:
items.note: Time, season and the inclination of the Astra's can stand against health.

items.quote: For whatsoever is cured before the time is subject to a relaps tis a very instant of the Season or time of the harvest only that makes a sure and certaine cure
items.note: A cure before its time relapses; only the right instant, called the time of the harvest, makes a sure cure.

items.quote: A ripe pear or apple will fall of its own accord, but before wee shake the tree in vaine to get it down.
items.note: The ripe fruit stands as a likeness for the right time of a cure; the paragraph applies it to cures itself.

items.quote: especially in the cure of Astrall diseases
items.note: The text sets apart a kind of disease by this name, in whose cure time and season matter most.

items.quote: make it their chiefe care that they doe no hurt when they can doe no good
items.note: Physicians should take care that they and their Physick do not hurt more than the disease.

items.quote: In cures respect is to be had to the season, for in summer one course is to be taken, in winter another, in Autumn another.
items.note: Margin note: the course of a cure differs by season.

items.quote: Sixthly, Because diseases are come to their appoynted period, and then by the Lawes of Nature there can be no recovery
items.note: Sixth cause: the disease has reached its appointed period.

items.quote: as in perfect, absolute and compleat bituminous, Colar, stony and sandy coagulations
items.note: Examples of consummated diseases without cure are named as kinds of 'coagulations'; those born blind and deaf follow as a further example.

items.quote: For what Nature hath once taken away the Physitian can by no means restore,
items.note: What nature has taken away the physician cannot restore.

items.quote: None can reform the errours of Nature.
items.note: Margin note states the same point briefly.

items.quote: Seventhly, As the base nigardlynesse of the sick
items.note: Seventh cause opens with the niggardliness of the sick, which makes the physician negligent.

items.quote: the sick parties doubt, distrust, and unbeliefe of the Physitians diligence and care, doth either retard the effect of the Physick, or altogether hinder the endeavor of the Physitian
items.note: The patient's doubt and unbelief slow or hinder the Physick.

items.quote: think to be made well by God (though indeed he be the onely Physitian) without the use of Means by which he worketh
items.note: Croll rejects refusing Physick in trust that God heals without means; God is called the only physician, working by means.

items.quote: There is a twofold Physick; Visible or created, and Invisible even the WORD of GOD:
items.note: The text says Physick is twofold: visible or created, and invisible, which is the Word of God.

items.quote: he that saith Physick is worth nothing, doth upon the matter affirm that there is no God
items.note: To despise Physick is set equal to despising God's Word.

items.quote: Physitians should take nothing of the poor for their Physick
items.note: Margin note: no payment from the poor; charity is to be the physician's chief virtue.

items.quote: Ecclesiastic: 38.
items.name: Ecclesiastic:
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside 'We ought not to resist the Ordinance of God'.

items.quote: The Physitian and the Physick are the very true mercy of God.
items.note: Margin note calls physician and Physick the mercy of God.

items.quote: Moreover, as hath been said, the Mind of the Patient being raised with much confidence doth take the Physick with a stronger desire
items.note: Points back to an earlier place in this writing on the patient's confidence.

items.quote: it was not without cause that Hippocrates in his Aphorismes speaketh so much of the Confidence of the sick in the Physitian and his Physick.
items.name: Hippocrates
items.note: Hippocrates' Aphorismes are named as speaking much of the confidence of the sick.

items.quote: A firm Faith, undoubted Hope, Love and Confidence toward the Physitian and his Physick, doth very much conduce to health, yea sometimes more than the Physitian and his Physick too.
items.note: Faith and confidence in physician and Physick help health, sometimes more than these themselves.

items.quote: Naturall Faith (I speak not of the Faith of Grace by Christ) inborn of God the Father in the first Creation, which is our IMAGINATION, is so powerfull that it can both cause and cure diseases
items.note: The text says what Naturall Faith is: inborn at the first creation, 'which is our IMAGINATION'; it can cause and cure diseases.

items.quote: (I speak not of the Faith of Grace by Christ)
items.note: The text itself says in which sense 'Faith' is not meant here.

items.quote: it breedeth that Basilisk of Heaven, which intoxicateth the microcosmicall Firmament
items.note: In time of pestilence the imagination, from fear, is said to breed a thing so named, which poisons the 'microcosmicall Firmament'.

items.quote: The Naturall Plague becomes Firmamental and supernaturall, that is to say, when the Iliaster or Evestrum of the Sun, provoked by the sins of men to wrath and punishment, infecteth and punisheth mortall men
items.note: The text explains with 'that is to say' how the natural plague becomes Firmamental and supernatural: through the 'Iliaster or Evestrum of the Sun' and the influx of the stars.

items.quote: because of the singular participarion it hath with the Evester of Man
items.note: The Evestrum of the Sun is said to have a share in common with 'the Evester of Man'; the lines given do not say what an Evester is.

items.quote: nor is there any medicine so potent that can resist and help against it
items.note: No medicine is strong enough against this kind of plague.

items.quote: it infecteth the Mummy and Sulphur of the microcosm, Man, who hiddenly possesseth all innate macrocosmicall poysons
items.note: Man, named the microcosm, is said to hold hidden in him all the poisons of the macrocosm; what is infected is his 'Mummy and Sulphur'.

items.quote: merry heart is a continuall feast.
items.note: Margin note beside the passage on the patient's confidence; its first letters are a gap.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside 'sorrow is the venome of Life'.

items.quote: The Stars are the rods of the Astra's.
items.note: Margin note says what the stars are in relation to the Astra's: their rods.

items.quote: Paracels. tract. 2.
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: Margin note names a tract of Paracelsus beside the passage on the plague; its title has gaps.

items.quote: Such is the force of the Sydereall spirit upon the body, that whithersoever it imagineth and dreameth it carryeth and leadeth the very body up and down with it, as we see in Noctambulaters.
items.note: The 'Sydereall spirit' leads the body where it imagines; sleep-walkers are the example.

items.quote: God can no otherwayes be overcome but by Faith
items.note: Faith is said to be the only way God is overcome; whoever believes in God works by God.

items.quote: but how that comes to passe cannot be searched out
items.note: The text says the manner in which faith works by God cannot be searched out.

items.quote: Faith is at least a work, I mean his work in whom we believe.
items.note: With 'I mean' the text says in what sense faith is called a work: the work of him who is believed in.

items.quote: The Cogitations surpasse and goe beyond the Operations of the Astra's and Elements
items.note: Thoughts joined with faith are placed above the workings of Astra's and elements.

items.quote: the Imagination giveth a Sydus or Constellation, the Sydus, (by reason of the Matrimony with the Imagination) giveth the effect or work.
items.note: A chain is stated: Faith gives the Imagination, the Imagination a 'Sydus or Constellation', the Sydus the effect. 'Sydus' is given 'Constellation' as its other name.

items.quote: The Will and Imagination of Man is the mother of the plague; so that a Man by his Imagination may infect a whole country with the Plague.
items.note: Margin note: man's will and imagination are the mother of the plague.

items.quote: Read Paracel of invisible diseases, and the efficacy of the faith of Nature, which by God can do all things Naturally.
items.name: Paracel
items.note: Margin note sends the reader to Paracelsus on invisible diseases and on 'the faith of Nature'.

items.quote: To mix Faith with the Physick is that which giveth spirit to the Physick, the spirit gives the knowledge of the Physick, the Physick gives health.
items.note: A second chain: faith mixed with Physick gives it spirit, the spirit gives knowledge of the Physick, the Physick gives health.

items.quote: according to his Faith so doth the Spirit further and assist him, I mean the Spirit of Nature or the Sydus of the medicine.
items.note: The text says which Spirit it means: the Spirit of Nature, or the Sydus of the medicine.

items.quote: A man many times through the Faith of Imagination doth that which the best Physitians with their chiefest medicaments cannot do
items.note: The 'Faith of Imagination' is said to do what the best physicians and medicines cannot.

items.quote: as we saw some years since in that famous Anwalding Panacaea
items.note: Named as an example where persuasion cured more than the medicine's own virtue.

items.quote: that new medicinall Spring which brake out this yeare in the coasts of Misnia and Bohemia
items.note: A second example of the same, placed by the text in 'this yeare'.

items.quote: For which there can be no other reason given but the constant excessive affection of them that use it
items.note: Croll gives the users' strong affection as the only reason for these cures.

items.quote: For the rational soul rouzed up and inflamed with a vehement imagination overcometh even Nature it selfe
items.note: The soul inflamed by imagination overcomes nature and causes sickness or health in its own body and in others.

items.quote: He that falls mad by the biting of a mad dogg will have the shape of doggs appearing in his urine
items.note: An example given for the power of imagination on the body.

items.quote: For by her Imagination she formeth the infant, as a Potter doth the clay.
items.note: The imagination of a woman with child is said to form the infant and mark it with the thing longed for.

items.quote: then the Astra's of the microcosmicall Firmament, or the Astra's of the humane Mind are moved with the
items.note: 'The Astra's of the microcosmicall Firmament' is given 'the Astra's of the humane Mind' as its other name.

items.quote: just as the externall Astra's of the microcosmicall Firmament
items.note: The comparison names 'microcosmicall Firmament' on both sides: for the Astra's of the human mind and for the 'externall Astra's'. The lines given do not show how the two sides differ.

items.quote: the Astra's of the Imagination of the great bellied women doe print an Influence and impression upon the child, as Engravers mark their work with an iron stamp
items.note: The imprint on the child is described as an influence of the Astra's of the imagination, like an engraver's stamp.

items.quote: The Imagination is like pitch, it easily sticketh
items.note: Margin note likens the imagination to pitch; its end has a gap.

items.quote: There are impressions of the inferior
items.note: Margin note beside the passage on impressions; the rest is gaps.

items.quote: many through overmuch joy or too much sorrow, by too much love or hatred, have dyed, and many times by the like passions have been cured of long diseases
items.note: Vehement affections of the mind can kill and can cure.

items.quote: as Avicen saith, Nature obeyeth the cogitations and vehement desires of the Soul, and when the spirit is affected, the body in which the spirit lies hid, is affected also
items.name: Avicen
items.note: Words given to Avicen: nature obeys the soul's desires; the spirit is said to lie hid in the body.

items.quote: good words are the Physitians of a sick Soul.
items.note: Margin note: better the body sick than the soul; good words heal a sick soul.

items.quote: In lib. de Anima.
items.name: lib. de Anima
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside the passage that cites Avicen.

items.quote: although it can do all things; yet ought it to keep and observe the property of the Image
items.note: Margin note on Natural Faith: though it can do all things, it ought to keep the property of the Image; the words before have gaps.

items.quote: Unbeliefe is the greatest and most powerfull enemy of Faith: For the Imagination joyned with Faith can do all things.
items.note: Margin note: unbelief is faith's chief enemy; imagination joined with faith can do all things.

items.quote: Againe, the aforesaid Naturall Faith its efficacy manifested it selfe in the woman that had the bloody issue, and in the Centurion.
items.note: Points back to the Naturall Faith named in CH5.75 and gives two examples of it.

items.quote: hath great things in his hands and power, Gen. 32.25, 26.
items.name: Gen.
items.note: A writing is named in the text for the statement that man, made in God's image, has great things in his power.

items.quote: even so great, that in false intense opinions and operations, it worketh miracles
items.note: A constant credulity with strong imagination is said to work miracles even in false opinions.

items.quote: haesitation of Credulity and diffidence doe not onely shatter and break the vertue or force of the operating mind, which is the mean between both extreams
items.note: Hesitation and distrust break the force of the operating mind and weaken every work, 'as well in Superstition as in true Religion'.

items.quote: our Saviour, as Holy Writ saith, was not able to work miracles in Capernaum, because they believed not, but with their incredulity and false faith resisted him.
items.name: Holy Writ
items.note: Holy Writ is named for the statement that unbelief hindered miracles in Capernaum.

items.quote: so likewise God will doe nothing without Man, as his Organ or Instument, God and the Creature both together, neither without the other.
items.note: Croll: as man can do nothing without God, God will do nothing without man as his instrument.

items.quote: no Man ought to will without God, because no Man can Be without God, in whom we are, and live, and are moved
items.note: No one ought to will without God.

items.quote: Mar. 13.58. Marke 6.5.
items.name: Mar.; Marke
items.note: Margin note names the writings beside the statement on Capernaum.

items.name: Mat.
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside 'God will doe nothing without Man'.

items.quote: Eightly, Least the sick party recovering should commit greater sins against God, his neighbor and himselfe to the losse of his Soul
items.note: Eighth and last cause: recovery would lead the sick to greater sins.

items.quote: for every sicknesse is as it were an expiation or propitiatory of sacrifice
items.note: Every sickness is called, 'as it were', an expiation: a call to amendment or a fatherly visitation.

items.quote: For health is nothing worth, seeing it is but condemnation to us, if our sins be not forgiven.
items.note: Health without forgiveness of sins is said to be worth nothing.

items.quote: sins weaken the powers of the Soul, and make it impotent to the Naturall Government of the body
items.note: Sins weaken the soul's government of the body, so the body's powers fail.

items.quote: as by a wholsome Purgatory (though few are reformed by their sicknesse)
items.note: Sickness is called a Purgatory by likeness ('as by'): a yoke and bridle that cuts off the licence of sinning.

items.name: Job
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside the passage on sickness as a bridle.

items.quote: no Corporall medicine (because God hath shut the doors of Nature) can do any good, but onely Celestiall and spirituall
items.note: For diseases arising from the wrath of God no bodily medicine helps, only heavenly and spiritual; 'God hath shut the doors of Nature'.

items.quote: by serious repentance, heartily to bewaile the sins that we have committed, to allay the provoked wrath of God by Amendment of life and Reconciliation to our neighbor
items.note: What the spiritual medicine consists of, introduced by 'viz.': repentance, amendment of life, reconciliation to the neighbour and to God, submission of the will.

items.quote: our Saviour the Celestiall Physitian of our Soules
items.what: the Celestiall Physitian of our Soules
items.note: The Saviour is named a physician, of souls.

items.quote: Paracelsus calleth them Deal diseases, which are from the Ens of God, who inflicteth all such diseases, and who alone worketh by good and bad men
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The name 'Deal diseases' is given to Paracelsus, with what it means: diseases from the Ens of God.

items.quote: the Cure, saith he, is by Faith, or when the purging is perfected the Physitian may then try his skill
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus's words on their cure: by faith, or by the physician once the purging is perfected.

items.quote: The Causes of those diseases that are of the Ens of God are unsearchable, here the cure must be sought in Faith, not in Nature
items.note: The causes of these diseases are said to be unsearchable; their cure is to be sought in faith, not in nature.

items.quote: the predestinate Terme or period according to the Divine pleasure is to be observed
items.note: In the cure by faith too a predestined term or period is to be kept.

items.quote: A Physitian beginneth in appeasing Gods wrath.
items.note: Margin note: the physician's beginning is to appease God's wrath.

items.name: Job
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside the passage on diseases from the wrath of God.
